title: Moab's Downfall
english: …Israel was formidable and hard to face. So, with great bitterness and a love of mischief, they set about stripping him of his help and persuaded him to offend the God who is over all.

They kept this attitude to the very end. Whenever Israel had offended God and happened to fall into misfortune, they boasted over him and jeered, charging God with being utterly powerless, the God who promises to save those who worship him.

The blessed Jeremiah is witness to this in his vision against them, where he says: “The horn of Moab is broken, and his arm is shattered. Make him drunk, for he magnified himself against the Lord” (Jeremiah 48:25–26). And again: “For thus says the Lord: Arioth is taken, and the strongholds are seized. And Moab will perish as a people, for he magnified himself against the Lord” (Jeremiah 48:40–42).

For in time the tyrant of the Assyrians and Babylonians came to lay Judea waste, and he took the cities of Samaria. The Moabites, for their part, smiled at those who had perished, mocked them beyond measure, and went on heaping insult on the glory of God.
For this reason they too have been given over to desolation and have utterly perished, cities, people, and every household together, so that now it seems almost as if they had never existed.
The vision before us, then, recalls what befell them, plainly by wrath from above, and says: “By night the Moabite will perish; for by night the wall of the land of Moab will perish” (Isaiah 15:1).

Some who have studied these matters closely have handed down that, when the Babylonians were about to make war on them, an earthquake struck and shook the chief city of the Moabites so violently that its whole wall fell of itself in the night and the dark. When this happened, before the enemy attacked, their hope of safety all but perished. That is why he says that the land of Moab will perish by night.

“But grieve,” he says, “over yourselves” (Isaiah 15:2). It is as if he said: Many times you raised your brows high and gloated over the misfortunes of others; but now the war is running against you yourselves, and the harm that comes of it hangs over your unholy heads. Grieve, then, not over any others, but over yourselves.

“For Lebedon will perish, where your altar is” (Isaiah 15:2). I said that the Moabites had become fierce and arrogant, trusting in the deceits of demons and supposing that by the magician's art they would prevail over the power of all, even of Israel himself, though God should defend him. So in the place called Lebedon they had an altar and a sacred precinct of no ordinary construction. There they performed their divinations and prided themselves greatly, and they held the place more sacred than any other. But, he says, even the workshop of your divination will perish.
“There you will go up…” (Isaiah 15:2)
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section begins mid-sentence; the clause before it ('For since, with God defending them, …') ends the previous section.
Jeremiah 48:40–42 follows Cyril's Greek, which agrees with the Septuagint (Jeremiah 31 there); 'Arioth' is the Septuagint form of Kerioth.
Lebedon is Cyril's spelling of the Septuagint Debon (Dibon) in Isaiah 15:2. The section ends inside the next verse Cyril quotes from Isaiah.

title: The Futility of Moab's Idols
english: …For I proclaim your sufferings and make widely known the calamity brought upon you. Like a well-tuned lyre I will cry out; I will strike the strings so, and make the song heard far and wide, as with the wall which you renewed.

At the beginning of the vision the blessed prophet said: “By night the land of Moab will perish; for by night the wall of the land of Moab will perish” (Isaiah 15:1). In explaining the force of these words, we said that when an earthquake struck, the wall of the land of Moab burst apart, and before the enemy's invasion it was all but levered up from its foundations and came crashing down over the land of the Moabites. They renewed it, but spent their labour on it entirely in vain, for the Assyrians and Babylonians took the whole land without effort.

“My inward parts,” he says, “will sound like a harp” over your misfortunes (Isaiah 16:11), and so I will make your suffering known far and wide, just as your wall came down, the wall you renewed, but to no good purpose. For when the wall fell of itself, what had happened escaped no one in the whole land of the Moabites, nor those living in other cities and countries.
“And it will be, when you are put to shame, that Moab has wearied herself at the altars; and she will go into her handmade things to pray, and she will not be able to deliver him” (Isaiah 16:12).

Something more, he says, will happen to you besides, which will bring you shame and disgrace: you will endure labours in vain, filling your altars with blood, making your sacrifices unceasing, and offering prayers to things made by hands. You will obtain nothing that brings help or safety, for they will not be able to free you from the evils hanging over you.

What strength is there in lifeless idols, which are inventions of human skill and have for their makers the very people who worship them? So, as the blessed David says: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8).

It should be known that the Moabites were extremely superstitious: readers of bird omens, false prophets, and tellers of wonders, who put very great confidence in the evils of sorcery. For they perhaps supposed that they could prevail over the enemy's power, not so much, I think, by skill in tactics as by the help of their own gods. But they were disappointed in their hope, since they called lifeless matter to their aid with sacrifices and prayer.

“This is the word which the Lord spoke against Moab, when he spoke” (Isaiah 16:13). This, he says, is the vision spoken by God against the land of the Moabites; “when he spoke,” that is, even before the words came through me, he had spoken a great many things about her, and on countless…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section begins and ends mid-passage.
Psalm 115:8 is Psalm 113:16 in the Septuagint numbering.

title: God Scatters the Plunderers
english: …plainly, calling them a multitude of nations. They came upon the lands, that is, the cities of Judea, like a great flood of water rushing down with violence and raising a roar, all but sweeping over those who resisted like the waves of the sea.
Here he calls them “the back of many nations” (Isaiah 17:12), because many nations were pursued by them; and pursuers always and everywhere run at the backs of those who flee.

Then what follows? “He will drive him off,” he says, that is, he will send him back, “and pursue him far away, like the fine chaff of winnowers before the wind, and like the dust of a wheel which a storm carries” (Isaiah 17:13). For what is so easily scattered as dust from a wheel and a threshing floor when a fierce wind sweeps down on it?

That Sennacherib went off a fugitive, the God of all will confirm when he says to him through the voice of Isaiah: “I will put a muzzle in your nose and a bridle in your lips, and I will turn you back by the way by which you came” (Isaiah 37:29).
“Toward evening there will be mourning; before morning it will be no more. This is the portion of those who plundered you, and the inheritance of those who inherited you” (Isaiah 17:14).

I said earlier that Rabshakeh surrounded Jerusalem with his fighting force and threatened to take it before long, but perished with his whole army before dawn and daylight. So there will be mourning toward evening, he says, since those in Jerusalem no doubt expected the assault of the war to come in the morning; but it ended before dawn.

That is why he says: There will be mourning toward evening, but before morning it will be no more. That is, the weeping will stop and come to an end, and it will vanish together with the fear of suffering, since God comes to their help, destroys the enemy's ranks beyond all expectation, and drives their leader out of the land of the Jews besides.
The blessed David also explains this when he says: “At evening weeping will stay the night, and at morning there will be gladness” (Psalm 30:5).

But this, he says, is the lot, this the portion of those who plundered you and seized you as their own inheritance. By these words he reproaches the people of Israel: they themselves had done the things for which the nation might well have perished utterly, yet he takes pity on them once more and punishes with death those who plunder the people allotted to him.

For, it says, “when the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and his people Jacob became the Lord's portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:8–9).

But besides this, consider this point carefully with me, and pass, as it were, from the events of history to the inmost meanings. When the wicked and hostile powers, pouring over the soul like violent water, either by trials from without…
